items.title: Article: The Evolution of Agentic Harnesses: From Chains to Graph to Code
items.summary:
Agentic LLM systems have moved from linear prompt chains to graph-based workflows and, more recently, code-executing harnesses. Chains are simple but fragile, graphs add branching, retries, and validation, and code harnesses verify outputs through execution. The article advises validating model outputs and choosing the least complex design that meets reliability, speed, and cost needs.

By Karthik Ramgopal

items.title: Frontier-OPD: Discovering the Edge of Agent Capability and Teaching Agents to Go Beyond
items.summary: On-policy distillation aligns teacher feedback with a student's current behavior, yet acquiring useful supervision for multi-turn agents requires identifying both where guidance is needed and whether the student can sustain the interaction afterward. We introduce Frontier-OPD, which addresses this problem through the student's learning frontier: decision situations that remain challenging but admit useful autonomous continuation after brief teacher guidance. To operationalize this frontier, Frontier-OPD organizes on-policy experience into a shared-state trajectory graph, where trajectory-balanced aggregation of teacher-student disagreement identifies distinct intervention candidates while preserving the histories needed for replay. Short teacher bridges are then assessed by comparing agreement over the bridge and the ensuing student continuation with an equally long segment of the original trajectory, providing a behavioral proxy for guidance that the current student can build on. Accepted teacher responses augment ordinary distillation data, and fresh rollouts renew the frontier estimate as the policy changes. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld report higher mean autonomous performance than the compared distillation baselines across the evaluated student scales and teacher configurations, with ablations indicating complementary effects of candidate selection and guidance filtering. In one ALFWorld timing setting, the additional collection cost is offset by a shorter time to a target success rate.

items.title: HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvement for Harness Token Efficiency
items.summary: Agent harnesses repeatedly invoke reasoning after tool feedback, even when an earlier call has already fixed the next action. We introduce HarnessMM (Harness Minus Minus), a method for improving harness token efficiency through guarded decision reuse and recursive self-improvement (RSI). RSI iteratively refines companion harness configurations from training feedback, with validation selecting the configuration for deployment. A controller at the model-tool boundary reuses resolved decisions to replace later reasoning callbacks while actor weights remain fixed. Executable Decision Graphs store exact actions, literal arguments, causal dependencies, and public guards. Guarded Decision Reuse activates these persistent decisions from observed receipts; Certified Callback Substitution executes them through the native interface and records removal of the registered slow callback. New semantic decisions, unsupported evidence, and selector abstention invoke the original actor again. The representation restricts what feedback may change, while complete-task measurements establish quality and cost. On HumanEval, HarnessMM preserves Codex success at 90.82\% while reducing Tokens/task (k) from 66.72 to 47.02 (29.54\% saving). For DeepSeek Harness, success rises from 71.43\% to 85.71\% while Tokens/task (k) fall from 96.28 to 11.62 (87.93\% saving). A separate MBPP ablation measures 26.91\% lower cost than single-use graphs and 19.52\% lower cost than retained callbacks. These results establish guarded decision reuse as a practical way to reduce repeated reasoning in existing harnesses.

items.title: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
items.summary: Agents and verifiers often rely on the text a tool prints, and that text can misrepresent what the tool actually did, even when the tool's computation is correct. We saw this happen in a production RAG research system used by the Pilsudski Institute in New York, where tool output formatters misled an agent into giving wrong or incomplete information to users. Each tool did its job correctly, but its output omitted search limits, result caps, or identifier namespaces. We also recreated an unlabeled estimate caught in code review before release. We studied whether these formatters misled agents and verifiers and how much the repaired wording helps. We fed tool results to agents using two formatter versions: one with the key omissions and one with all missing details clearly stated. That difference alone changed what the agents claimed and what the verifiers accepted. Unsupported agent claims dropped substantially for three of the four failure types. In one test, verifiers went from accepting incorrect answers 90 out of 90 times to rejecting them 90 out of 90 times. A control showed the verifiers could catch the errors once they were given the missing facts and asked to judge correctness. We include the audit prompt we used with Codex and Claude Code in an exploratory demonstration, written with prior knowledge of our own system's defects. When pointed at an old version of our own system, it rediscovered the defects that were still live and surfaced twelve more we had not catalogued. When pointed at OpenClaw and Hermes, two of the best-known open-source agentic systems, it found warped formatters in both. We opened PRs to fix both, and the OpenClaw fix has already been merged. Practitioners can run the same prompt on their own systems today.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.310
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added the Monitor tool and plugin monitors on Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry, and when telemetry or nonessential traffic is disabled; long foreground sleeps are now blocked there too
  • Fixed requests failing behind some gateways and compatible servers that reject the effort-2025-11-24 beta value or mid-conversation system messages; Claude Code now retries without them
  • Fixed background cleanup deleting some recent files, such as pasted images, when cleanupPeriodDays is set to a very large value
  • Fixed compaction after a "Prompt is too long" error keeping too much of a conversation with dense text, such as base64 or SVG, so the next request could fail again
  • Fixed file read permission prompts not showing where a symbolic link leads
  • Fixed a question's auto-continue timeout firing the moment the external editor closed after a long edit
  • Windows: Fixed PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks letting a tool call through when Git Bash is missing and the hook's command is only quoted strings, such as a quoted path
  • Improved auto mode's prompt before the first read outside the working directories: it now says when blocking those reads makes shell commands ask for permission
  • Improved memory use of non-interactive sessions (-p, Agent SDK) during compaction when the transcript file is very large
  • Improved a mod's Image to draw inside tmux with allow-passthrough and focus-events on, in kitty, Ghostty, and iTerm2 3.5+ with fullscreen rendering, where it showed only its alt text
  • Linux: Improved /sandbox and the sandbox startup warning to name Ubuntu's AppArmor restriction on user namespaces, and how to lift it, when it keeps bubblewrap from starting the sandbox
  • Changed the error for an MCP tool call that times out in a non-interactive session while the server's elicitation is unanswered: it now tells Claude that no answer came and not to repeat the call
  • [VSCode] Fixed pressing Enter on the plan review card's "Send feedback and keep planning" button approving the plan instead of sending your comments back
  • [VSCode] Fixed the panel showing "Something went wrong" after "Switch branch & continue" on a cloud session opened from Session history's Web tab
  • [Cloud sessions] Added Claude Code cloud sessions and Remote Control permissions to Enterprise custom roles, so Owners can control access to each by role
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a Choose file button to load a cloud environment's setup script from a file
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed failed saves and archives in the cloud environment edit dialog showing no error inside the dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed failed routine API token actions showing only a toast; the error now appears in the routine edit dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the session start checklist to show a cloud environment's setup script output in a scrolling box
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed turning on Cloud sessions or Remote Control in admin settings to ask for confirmation and list the custom roles that have that permission
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed the cloud environment dialog to open network access, setup script and environment variables from rows instead of listing every editor at once
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag treating ! commands such as !restart and !help as ordinary messages when sent in bold, italic or strikethrough
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag admin channel and workspace pages being replaced by a load error when a background refresh of the bundle list fails
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag's spend limits page in admin settings reporting that no channels match a filter while channel names are still loading
  • [Code Review] Fixed the Code Review admin section hiding its repositories and switches after a failed refresh of the repository list
  • [Code Review] Improved the Code Review admin section to retry the first load and show one Try again banner when it still fails

items.title: Interpretable sparse fine-tuning with TopKLoRA enables faithful circuit discovery
items.summary: Fine-tuning on datasets of unknown origin can create a backdoor in the trained model when the data includes poisoned examples. Difficult to localise and remove, backdoors can persist through safety training. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods capture the full parameter changes introduced during training, they are not easily interpretable. We present the full method of TopKLoRA, extending the preliminary proposal of Masiak et al. (2025), an interpretable-by-design LoRA variant in which only the $k$ largest adapter latents are active at each token. Unlike SAEs, TopKLoRA is trained purely on downstream loss, where optimisation pressure incentivises learning functionally causal latents. We demonstrate this sparse LoRA adapter in a sleeper-agent backdoor case study where we create model organisms by fine-tuning gemma-2-2b, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen2.5-7B on a poisoned instruction-following dataset. For each organism, we identify and ablate a circuit that is both necessary and sufficient to implement the backdoor. Furthermore, our new fine-tuning method produces sparse circuits that are up to an order of magnitude smaller than a dense LoRA baseline, allowing surgical ablation of the malicious capability without sacrificing instruction-following performance. Finally, we propose a technique to construct model organisms with localised circuits using TopKLoRA latents and gradient-routing, which we use to validate the findings of our circuit search algorithm. We consider these findings as a step toward interpretable-by-design architectures that provide faithful units of analysis without compromising model performance. We share our code: https://github.com/interpretable-finetuning/TopKLoRA.

items.title: Profile-Driven User Simulation via Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Rewards for Task-Oriented Dialogues
items.summary: Building Task-Oriented Dialogue (TOD) systems for high-value scenarios such as financial marketing requires large volumes of domain-specific dialogue data, which privacy regulations, annotation costs, and the need for expert labor make hard to obtain. User simulation offers a remedy, but existing methods target general-domain dialogue and exhibit two key limitations: insufficient modeling of domain-specific business processes and compliance constraints, and inadequate capture of the colloquial, spoken-language character of voice interactions. We propose ProfileSim, a profile-driven user simulation framework for financial marketing outbound calls. It jointly models user profiles---demographics and Big Five personality traits---and business profiles---intents reverse-engineered from real call logs---enabling fine-grained control over simulated behavior. The base model is fine-tuned on real voice dialogue data and refined by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with hierarchical rewards at the dialogue and utterance levels. Paired with a customer service agent integrating Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) constraints and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), ProfileSim achieves the highest colloquial naturalness, the strongest user profile adherence and the lowest agent score on long-tail intents among all evaluated user generators, while producing substantially shorter user utterances at comparable business compliance. The generated dialogue data is designed to support intent recognition training, agent evaluation, and rapid cold-start deployment.

items.title: Expanding Claude availability and deployment choice on Google Cloud
items.summary:
Every organization has unique requirements for building and scaling generative AI. At Google Cloud, we are committed to giving developers model choice and architectural flexibility to run workloads however they need.

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of an Anthropic-managed deployment option for Claude Models on Google Cloud. This gives teams more choice in how they run their models, helping them consolidate AI workloads on Google Cloud alongside our existingGoogle-managed deployment option. 

Both options deliver the same frontier models on day zero, the same pricing, and the same Google Cloud billing. The difference comes down to who acts as your data processor and whether you need access to the new Claude platform features when they launch:

[NEW] Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed)

Delivers day-zero access to Claude models and Claude Platform features such as Claude Managed Agents (beta), skills, and code execution. Anthropic operates the stack as the data processor on Google Cloud infrastructure under Anthropic’s terms of service, while organizations authenticate with Google Cloud IAM, maintain Cloud Audit Logging, and consolidate spend under their existing Google Cloud billing and eligible commitments.

Learn more: Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic-managed).

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed)

Continues to deliver day-zero access to the latest Claude models with strict governance, compliance, and sovereignty requirements. Google Cloud operates as the data processor under existing customer agreements, providing VPC Service Controls, Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK), and data residency in the U.S., EU, and APAC. New Claude Platform features roll out over time as they are integrated into the Google-managed infrastructure. Teams also benefit from native integrations with Google Cloud services like BigQuery and Model Armor, along with standard billing and eligible commitment drawdown. 

Learn more: Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed)

No matter how you choose to deploy, you can access Anthropic's latest frontier models on Google Cloud, including Claude Fable 5.1, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and Opus 5.5, with new platform features available immediately on the Anthropic-managed option and rolling out on the Google-managed option once integrated. This gives developers the full spectrum of reasoning, coding, and multi-modal capabilities with Google Cloud IAM and Marketplace billing. Get started.
